stories.title: Piracetam attenuates cyclophosphamide-evoked pulmonary injury in rats; the role of AMPK/NF-κB/NLRP3/caspase-1 and caspase-3 mediated apoptosis signaling cascades
stories.description: Cyclophosphamide (CP) is often employed in the treatment of numerous malignancies and autoimmune diseases, although it is accompanied by numerous side effects. Piracetam (PIRA) is used as a nootropic agent and reported to possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties in addition to its established cognitive-enhancing effects. This study aimed to investigate the potential protective effects of PIRA against CP-induced lung damage in rats. CP was utilized to provoke pulmonary damage. Molecular docking was performed to predict the binding affinity of piracetam for NF-κB p65, NLRP3, caspase-1, caspase-3, and AMPK. Arterial blood gas parameters (PaO₂ and PaCO₂) were assessed to evaluate pulmonary gas-exchange function. The lung contents of MDA, GSH, and CAT activity were measured. Levels of lung IL-18, IL-1β, TNF-α, and caspase-1 were evaluated using ELISA. Immunohistochemistry was employed to evaluate NF-κB p65 and caspase-3. The Western blot technique was utilized to evaluate the protein expression of NLRP3 and p-AMPK. Lung Bax and Bcl-2 gene expression was assessed using qRT-PCR. The histological examination of lung tissues was conducted. Molecular docking revealed favorable binding affinities of piracetam. CP caused a notable reduction in PaO₂ and elevation in PaCO₂, alongside a notable increase in lung MDA, IL-18, IL-1β, TNF-α, caspase-1, and Bax levels, with a substantial reduction in GSH, CAT, p-AMPK, and Bcl-2. CP administration also led to the upregulation of NLRP3 protein. Additionally, the immunopositivity of both NF-κB p65 and caspase-3 was elevated in the CP group. PIRA markedly ameliorated all previously described functional, biochemical, and histopathological anomalies. PIRA pretreatment significantly improved CP-induced pulmonary injury, an effect associated with suppression of NF-κB/NLRP3/caspase-1 and caspase-3 signaling and with increased p-AMPK expression.

stories.title: Progressive decline in EEG low frequency spectral power during overnight sleep
stories.description: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone in the analysis of sleep architecture and sleep disorders. Prior studies describe decreases in EEG power towards the end of overnight sleep. However, most of these observations are based on small samples, rely in part on qualitative analyses, do not characterize EEG power at intermediate stages, and do not examine all sleep stages. Importantly, the possible relation between a dynamic change in EEG power and health outcomes was not explored. We sought to compute power in sleep stages for the first, middle, and last instances of sleep using automated, quantitative EEG methods leveraging 10,000 high-resolution overnight polysomnography cases. Results confirm that power in the 1–20 Hz range during the last instances of all sleep stages is significantly decreased compared to first instances. However, power increases in the delta and theta bands during the middle instances of N1 and N2. For N1, the decline in power follows a linear trend. These changes were not uniform across brain regions, and correlations between the EEG power decrease and clinical outcomes were statistically significant albeit with modest effect size. Thus, our work provides a rigorous, large-scale analysis of temporal trends of EEG power across the overnight sleep period, revealing novel dynamics and a potential impact on health beyond sleep disorders.
